Karl Marx was a German philosopher, economist and revolutionary whose critique of capitalism inspired socialist movements and, in the twentieth century, communist states that at their height ruled about a third of the world's people. With Friedrich Engels he wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848), and alone the first volume of Capital (1867).

He was born in Trier in the Rhineland to a Jewish family that had converted to Lutheranism. He studied law and philosophy, came under the influence of Hegel, and turned to radical journalism. Expelled from Germany, France and Belgium in turn, he settled in London in 1849 and lived there, often in poverty, for the rest of his life. His friend Engels, son of a mill owner, supported him.

His main ideas:

  • History is driven by how people produce their living, and by conflict between classes.
  • Under capitalism, workers sell their labour, and owners keep the surplus value it creates.
  • Capitalism is enormously productive but unstable, prone to crises, and creates its own gravediggers, the industrial working class.
  • It will be replaced, through revolution, by a classless communist society.

He wrote the Manifesto on the eve of the revolutions of 1848, and later helped lead the First International, a union of workers' groups. When he died in 1883, only a small crowd attended his funeral at Highgate Cemetery.

His influence came later. Social democratic parties built on his ideas, and Lenin used them to justify the Bolshevik revolution of 1917. Regimes calling themselves Marxist, under Stalin, Mao and others, became dictatorships that killed millions; how much of that follows from Marx is still argued.
